tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise background it so the user can interject. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

1	# wordstat: Interface Contract
2	
3	## Constraints
4	
5	- **Stack:** Python >=3.11, standard library only; pytest for tests only.
6	- **Package location:** `wordstat/` at repo root (flat layout, no `src/`).
7	- **Entry point:** `python -m wordstat ...` run from repo root.
8	
9	## Functional requirements
10	
11	- **R1** `python -m wordstat --help` exits 0.
12	- **R2** `python -m wordstat [--json] [--top N] FILE` reads exactly one file, decoded as UTF-8 with an optional BOM (`utf-8-sig`). stdin is never read.
13	- **R3** Counts, computed on the decoded text:
14	  - `lines` = `len(text.splitlines())`
15	  - `words` = number of matches of `[a-z0-9]+` in `text.lower()`
16	  - `chars` = `len(text)` (code points, BOM excluded)
17	- **R4** `top` lists the `N` most frequent words (same tokens as R3), ordered by count descending, then word ascending. `--top` defaults to 3. Fewer than `N` distinct words lists all of them.
18	- **R5** Default output is the text format; `--json` selects the JSON format.
19	- **R6** Output is deterministic: UTF-8, `\n` line endings, no locale use. stdout is reconfigured to `encoding="utf-8", newline="\n"`.
20	
21	## Interface contract
22	
23	### Command
24	
25	```
26	python -m wordstat [--json] [--top N] FILE
27	```
28	
29	- argparse `prog` is `wordstat`.
30	- `--top` must be an integer >= 1, else usage error.
31	
32	### Text format
33	
34	Exactly four lines, each ending in `\n`:
35	
36	```
37	lines: <lines>
38	words: <words>
39	chars: <chars>
40	top: <word>=<count> <word>=<count> ...
41	```
42	
43	With no words, the last line is `top:` with no trailing space.
44	
45	### JSON format
46	
47	One line: the result of `json.dumps(obj)` with default separators, followed by `\n`, where `obj` has keys in this order:
48	
49	```
50	{"lines": <int>, "words": <int>, "chars": <int>, "top": [{"word": <str>, "count": <int>}, ...]}
51	```
52	
53	### Exit codes and errors
54	
55	Errors print one line to stderr, prefix `wordstat: error: `, and leave stdout empty. `<path>` is the FILE argument exactly as given.
56	
57	| Condition | Exit | stderr (after prefix) |
58	|---|---|---|
59	| File missing, a directory, or unreadable | 3 | `<path>: cannot read file` |
60	| Not valid UTF-8 | 3 | `<path>: not valid UTF-8` |
61	| Usage error (missing FILE, unknown flag, bad `--top`) | 2 | argparse default; the last stderr line must match `^wordstat: error: ` |
62	
63	Exit 0 on success, including an empty file. Exit 1 is reserved for unexpected internal errors.
64	
65	## Example
66	
67	`sample.txt` (UTF-8, `\n` endings):
68	
69	```
70	The cat sat.
71	The cat ran!
72	A dog.
73	```
74	
75	`python -m wordstat sample.txt` → exit 0, stdout:
76	
77	```
78	lines: 3
79	words: 8
80	chars: 33
81	top: cat=2 the=2 a=1
82	```
83	
84	`python -m wordstat --json --top 2 sample.txt` → exit 0, stdout:
85	
86	```
87	{"lines": 3, "words": 8, "chars": 33, "top": [{"word": "cat", "count": 2}, {"word": "the", "count": 2}]}
88	```

# Research report: wordstat CLI (Python 3.11)

I wrote this from knowledge of the docs and checked the argparse and regex claims with a throwaway `python3 -I -c` run. No files were created. Two limits on the checks:
- The local interpreter is **Python 3.9.6**, because 3.11 isn't installed here. The behaviours below are stable from 3.9 to 3.11, except where I flag it.
- I did no web fetches. The URLs under Sources are the pages these facts come from, but I did not re-read them.

## Key findings

### 1. argparse
1. `ArgumentParser(prog="wordstat")` makes usage and error lines start with `wordstat:`. Without `prog`, it uses `sys.argv[0]`, which is `__main__.py` under `python -m`. So set `prog` explicitly.
2. `parser.error()` prints the usage line to stderr, then `wordstat: error: <msg>`, and exits with code 2. The error line is always **last** on stderr. Checked:
   ```
   usage: wordstat [-h] [--json] [--top TOP] file
   wordstat: error: the following arguments are required: file
   ```
   Missing FILE, an unknown flag (`unrecognized arguments: --bogus`), and an extra positional (`unrecognized arguments: b`) all exit 2.
3. `type=` callables may raise `argparse.ArgumentTypeError(msg)`, `ValueError` or `TypeError`.
   - `ArgumentTypeError` keeps the custom message: `argument --top: must be >= 1`.
   - `ValueError` gives the generic `argument --top: invalid <name> value: 'x'`, where `<name>` is the callable's `__name__`.
   - Either way the result is exit 2 with the `wordstat: error: ` prefix.
4. **Negative values.** `--top -1` and `--top=-1` both reach the validator and fail with `must be >= 1`, exit 2. This works because the parser has no option strings that look like negative numbers, so `-1` is treated as a value, not a flag. The validator message is used, not "expected one argument". If the spec ever adds a numeric-looking short option, this changes.
5. `int()` is lenient, so a `type=int`-based validator accepts these:
   - `"+2"` gives 2.
   - `" 2 "` gives 2.
   - `"1_0"` gives 10.
   - Non-ASCII digits such as `"٣"` are also accepted.
   
   The contract says "integer >= 1", so these are valid. Leave them unrejected, or state the choice explicitly. `--top 0`, `--top x` and `--top 1.5` exit 2.
6. **Abbreviations.** `allow_abbrev` defaults to True, so `--to 2` is accepted as `--top` and `--js` as `--json`. The contract doesn't forbid this. Consider `allow_abbrev=False` for strictness, or leave the default and don't test it.
7. `--` ends option parsing, so `wordstat -- -f` reads a file named `-f`. A lone `-` is just a path string to argparse. The contract says stdin is never read, so `-` must be treated as a filename and produce `cannot read file`, exit 3, unless the file exists.
8. `exit_on_error=False` (added in 3.9) does **not** reliably suppress every error. It only affects `ArgumentError` raised during value parsing. Missing-required and unrecognized-argument errors still call `error()` and exit in 3.11. Don't use it. The default behaviour already matches the contract.
9. `--help` prints help to stdout and exits 0 (the `-h` action calls `parser.exit()`). `-h` also works.
10. The usage error for the `-1` case is separate from file errors. The contract says exit 3 for file errors, 2 for usage, and exit 1 for unexpected internal errors only.

### 2. Testing the CLI via subprocess in pytest
11. Use this call:
    `subprocess.run([sys.executable, "-m", "wordstat", *args], cwd=REPO_ROOT, capture_output=True)`
    - Omit `text=True` so `stdout` and `stderr` come back as **bytes**.
    - Byte-exact assertions then work, for example `r.stdout == b"lines: 3\nwords: 8\nchars: 33\ntop: cat=2 the=2 a=1\n"`.
    - Check `b"\r" not in r.stdout`. This matters mostly on Windows, where text-mode stdout would turn `\n` into `\r\n`. The contract's `newline="\n"` reconfigure fixes that.
12. Define `REPO_ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent`, with the tests in `tests/`. `python -m wordstat` only resolves the package because cwd is the repo root. Because `-m` puts cwd on `sys.path`, also pass `cwd=` explicitly rather than relying on how pytest was launched.
13. For hermetic runs, pass `env={**os.environ, "PYTHONUTF8": "0", "LC_ALL": "C", "PYTHONIOENCODING": ""}`.
    - This proves the output doesn't depend on locale (R6).
    - A second run with `PYTHONIOENCODING=latin-1` should still emit UTF-8, because of the explicit stdout reconfigure.
14. Use `timeout=` on `subprocess.run`, for example 30 seconds. Pass `stdin=subprocess.DEVNULL` to prove stdin is never read. A test could also give an open pipe and confirm the run doesn't hang.
15. **File fixtures.** `tmp_path` is a per-test `pathlib.Path`.
    - Write with `p.write_bytes(...)` for byte control. `write_text` applies newline translation on Windows.
    - For BOM tests: `b"\xef\xbb\xbf" + "abc".encode()` should give `chars` of 3.
    - Non-UTF-8 examples: `b"\xff\xfe"`, `b"\x80"`, and a truncated multibyte `b"\xe2\x82"`. All give exit 3 with `<path>: not valid UTF-8`.
    - Also cover UTF-16 text with a BOM, which isn't valid `utf-8-sig`.
16. **Path echo.** The error must echo the FILE argument exactly as given. Pass `str(p)` for absolute-path cases. Also test a relative path, with `cwd=tmp_path` and a name like `sub/x.txt` or `nope.txt`. Using `cwd=tmp_path` there conflicts with finding the package, so use `env PYTHONPATH=<repo>` in that case.
17. **Directory path.** Passing `tmp_path` gives `IsADirectoryError` on POSIX, but `PermissionError` on Windows. Catch `OSError` broadly to get exit 3 on both.
18. **Missing file.** `tmp_path / "nope.txt"` gives `FileNotFoundError`, a subclass of `OSError`. Exit 3 with `cannot read file`.
19. **Unreadable file.** `os.chmod(p, 0)` works on POSIX only.
    - On Windows, chmod only toggles read-only and doesn't block reads.
    - As root (CI containers), root bypasses permissions, so the read succeeds.
    - Guard with `@pytest.mark.skipif(sys.platform == "win32" or (hasattr(os, "geteuid") and os.geteuid() == 0), reason=...)`. Alternatively, probe at runtime with `os.access(p, os.R_OK)` after the chmod and `pytest.skip` if it's still readable.
    - Restore permissions in a `finally` so pytest's tmp cleanup works.
20. If the invalid file is a very large or sparse file, don't create one. Keep fixtures tiny.
21. Check empty-stdout on every error case: `r.stdout == b""`. Also check `r.stderr.endswith(b"\n")` and that the last line (`r.stderr.decode().splitlines()[-1]`) matches `^wordstat: error: `. For exit 3, stderr should be **exactly** one line: `wordstat: error: <path>: cannot read file\n`. A usage error has usage plus the error line.
22. Prefer `parametrize` for usage errors: `[]`, `["--top","0","f"]`, `["--top","-1","f"]`, `["--top","x","f"]`, `["--bogus","f"]`, `["a","b"]`. Each should give exit 2 and the regex match on the last line. Note that a usage error occurs **before** file access, so the file need not exist. Also the order of checks matters: `--top 0 missing.txt` gives 2, not 3.

### 3. Regex and Unicode quirks (verified)
23. `re.findall("[a-z0-9]+", text.lower())` is deterministic. Checked on `"İx K ſ ß ΣΑΣ".lower()` (the K there is U+212A KELVIN SIGN):
    - `"İ".lower()` is `i` + U+0307 (`b'i\xcc\x87'`). So `İx` gives tokens `i`, `x`, because the combining dot splits the word.
    - U+212A KELVIN SIGN `.lower()` gives ASCII `k`, so it **matches** as a word. This holds even though the glyph is not ASCII.
    - `ſ` (long s) lowercases to itself and does **not** match. `ß` and Greek letters aren't matched either.
    - Letters like `é` are not in `[a-z0-9]`, so `café` gives `caf`. `naïve` gives `na`, `ve`.
    - Non-ASCII digits (such as Arabic-Indic) don't match `[0-9]`, since the class is explicit.
    - Don't use `re.ASCII` or `\w`. The explicit class is correct as written.
24. `str.splitlines()` splits on more than `\n`: `\r`, `\r\n`, `\v`, `\f`, `\x1c`-`\x1e`, `\x85`, `\u2028`, `\u2029`. A test string `"a\r\nb\x0b\x0c\x1c\x85 c d"` gave 7 lines.
    - A trailing newline doesn't add a line: `"a\n"` has 1 line.
    - Empty text has 0 lines.
    - `"\n"` has 1 line.
    - Test these exactly.
25. **Newline translation on read.** Decode from bytes: `data.decode("utf-8-sig")`. Do **not** open in text mode, since universal newlines would translate `\r\n` to `\n` and change `chars` (the `\r` would be dropped). The contract says `chars = len(text)` on the decoded text, so read with `open(path, "rb")` or `Path.read_bytes()` and decode. Test a `\r\n` file: `chars` should count both characters.
26. `utf-8-sig` strips only a **leading** BOM. A BOM in the middle remains as U+FEFF and counts as a char. It isn't matched as a word.
27. Surrogates: `b"\xed\xa0\x80"` is invalid in strict UTF-8, so exit 3. `chars` counts code points. A non-BMP character such as emoji counts as 1.
28. Sorting: use `sorted(counts.items(), key=lambda kv: (-kv[1], kv[0]))`. Ties are broken by word ascending using plain code-point order. All tokens are ASCII, so there's no locale concern. Don't use `Counter.most_common` for ties. It orders ties by first insertion, not alphabetically.
29. `json.dumps(obj)` with defaults uses `ensure_ascii=True` and separators `", "` and `": "`. The tokens are ASCII anyway, so output is stable. Keys come out in insertion order, so build the dict in the order the contract gives.
30. **stdout reconfigure.** `sys.stdout.reconfigure(encoding="utf-8", newline="\n")` is available on `TextIOWrapper` since 3.7. Call it before any output. Alternatively, write bytes via `sys.stdout.buffer.write(s.encode("utf-8"))`. Both give identical bytes.
31. On error, no partial stdout may exist. Compute everything first, then write once.
32. Exit code from `main()`: use `sys.exit(main())`, and make `main` return an int. In `__main__.py`, guard with `if __name__ == "__main__":` or just call it, since `-m` runs `__main__.py` directly.
33. A bare `except Exception` returning 1 for internal errors is consistent with the contract. Catch `OSError` and `UnicodeDecodeError` narrowly, around read and decode only.

## Constraints the spec MUST respect
- `prog="wordstat"` explicitly. Usage errors must exit 2 via argparse defaults. The last stderr line must match `^wordstat: error: `.
- `--top` is validated at parse time, so the failure is a usage error (exit 2) and not exit 3. `-1` must produce exit 2. It does, via the validator.
- Read file as **bytes**, decode with `utf-8-sig`, with no newline translation. `chars` must count `\r`.
- Catch `OSError` broadly (missing, directory, permission) for `cannot read file`. `UnicodeDecodeError` is `not valid UTF-8`. Both exit 3 with empty stdout.
- Error path text is the FILE argument verbatim, not resolved or normalised.
- stdin is never read. `-` is an ordinary filename.
- Output is reconfigured to UTF-8 with `\n`, and nothing may use the locale. Text format has exactly four `\n`-terminated lines. With no words, the last line is exactly `top:` with no trailing space. JSON is one line from default `json.dumps`.
- Python 3.11 standard library only. pytest is allowed for tests only.
- The sample's `chars: 33` must hold. Check: `The cat sat.\nThe cat ran!\nA dog.\n` is 13 + 13 + 7 = 33, which includes the final `\n`.

## Recommendations for the spec
- State explicitly: **no** `exit_on_error=False`, and the default `allow_abbrev` is either accepted or disabled (pick one). If left alone, don't test abbreviations.
- Provide a validator named so the error reads naturally, for example `_positive_int` raising `ArgumentTypeError("must be an integer >= 1")`. The exact wording after the prefix is argparse-default and should be tested only by prefix, since the contract fixes only the prefix for usage errors.
- Say that `int()` leniency (`+2`, `" 2 "`, `1_0`) is accepted, or specify a stricter regex such as `^[0-9]+$` and test it. Pick one and document it.
- Add a test list covering: the two contract examples byte-exact (text and JSON); empty file (`lines: 0`, `words: 0`, `chars: 0`, `top:`) with exit 0 and the JSON form `"top": []`; BOM-only file; `\r\n` file; no trailing newline; `--top` larger than the distinct word count; tie-ordering; uppercase folding; digits (`a1 b2`, `007`); punctuation splitting (`don't` gives `don`, `t`); and the Unicode quirks from findings 23 and 24 (İ, Kelvin sign, é, ß).
- Add the error matrix from finding 22, including the check that stdout is empty and the exit code is exactly 2 or 3. Include `--help` (exit 0, stdout non-empty, stderr empty). Test options before and after FILE (`wordstat f --json`) as argparse allows both.
- Add a no-stdin test with `stdin=subprocess.DEVNULL`, and a determinism test that sets `LC_ALL=C` and `PYTHONIOENCODING=ascii` yet still gets UTF-8 stdout. Use a fixture word set that is ASCII-only, since the output tokens are all ASCII. The locale check is most meaningful for the path echo in stderr. Mention that a non-ASCII filename on stderr may not be UTF-8 under a C locale. The contract only says stdout is reconfigured. Consider whether stderr should also be reconfigured, and avoid non-ASCII filenames in tests if left unspecified.
- Mark the permission test as skippable (finding 19), and note that the directory test is portable only if `OSError` is caught broadly.
- Test files must use `sys.executable` and `cwd=REPO_ROOT`. Use a `run(*args, cwd=...)` helper that returns the `CompletedProcess` with bytes.

## Sources
- https://docs.python.org/3.11/library/argparse.html (ArgumentParser `prog`, `type=` with ArgumentTypeError, `exit_on_error`, `allow_abbrev`, negative-number handling, `--`)
- https://docs.python.org/3.11/library/subprocess.html (`run`, `capture_output`, `cwd`, `timeout`)
- https://docs.python.org/3.11/library/io.html#io.TextIOWrapper.reconfigure

- https://docs.python.org/3.11/library/codecs.html (`utf-8-sig`)
- https://docs.python.org/3.11/library/json.html#json.dumps
- https://docs.python.org/3.11/library/re.html
- https://docs.pytest.org/en/stable/how-to/tmp_path.html (`tmp_path`)
- https://docs.pytest.org/en/stable/how-to/skipping.html (`skipif`)
